original_question: Enumerate all honeycomb arrays, where a honeycomb array is equivalently a Costas array with exactly one dot on every bottom-left to top-right diagonal.
target_in_paper: Problem 24 in §8.2 ("Honeycomb arrays"): "Enumerate all honeycomb arrays." The paper sets this up via Definition 13 (the intrinsic hexagonal-grid definition) and Definition 14 (the equivalent Costas-array reformulation). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the exact open problem and is very close to the paper’s own square-grid phrasing: the official target is to enumerate all honeycomb arrays, and the paper explicitly reformulates a honeycomb array as a Costas array with the extra property that every bottom-left–top-right diagonal contains exactly one dot. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
missing_details: It does not give the original intrinsic definition from the paper: a honeycomb array is first defined on a hexagonal grid, with exactly one dot in each row in each of the three natural grid directions, for a board parameterized by r and having 2r+1 dots in total. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

If you use the square-grid reformulation, you should also define what a Costas array is: an n×n permutation array (equivalently, a bijection f:[n]→[n]) whose distance vectors are all distinct. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

The diagonal condition needs the paper’s specific hexagon-to-square embedding to be unambiguous; without saying that this is the §8.2 square embedding of the hexagonal board, the phrase "every bottom-left–top-right diagonal" is not fully stand-alone. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
The quantifier over size should be explicit: the problem asks for all such arrays over all admissible radii/orders, not for a fixed size. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

For full faithfulness to the paper, one may also record the intrinsic Costas-type condition on the hexagonal grid: no two line segments joining pairs of dots may have both the same length and the same slope; equivalently, the autocorrelation values are only 0, 1, or 2r+1. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))

Nearby context shows that this is a finite classification problem: the paper notes that no honeycomb array with 2r+1 ≥ 1289 exists, so only finitely many honeycomb arrays can exist; at the time, 12 were known up to symmetry. This context sharpens what "enumerate all" means. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
refined_question: Determine all honeycomb arrays: for each r ∈ N, classify every dot/blank configuration on a finite hexagonal board of diameter 2r+1 having exactly one dot in each row in each of the three natural directions of the hexagonal grid, and satisfying the Costas-type condition that no two line segments joining pairs of dots have both the same length and the same slope. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, under the hexagon-to-square bijection described in §8.2, classify all Costas arrays of order 2r+1 whose bottom-left–top-right diagonals each contain exactly one dot. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
justification: The draft is not aiming at a broader neighboring problem: it matches Problem 24 exactly. Section 8.2 first defines honeycomb arrays intrinsically on the hexagonal grid (Definition 13), then gives the precise equivalent Costas-array reformulation (Definition 14), and immediately states the open problem "Enumerate all honeycomb arrays." The only substantive omissions in the draft are the intrinsic hexagonal-grid definition, the underlying definition of a Costas array, the quantifier over all radii/orders, and the fact that the diagonal condition is tied to the paper’s specific square embedding. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1102.5727.pdf))
